text: `getent passwd 1301` only ever shows ONE name (whichever entry comes first in /etc/passwd) -- that's exactly the trap. Look at the raw file instead: `awk -F: '$3==1301 {print}' /etc/passwd` lists every entry that actually uses that UID.

You should see both `logshipper` and `metricsagent` claiming UID 1301. Check `ls -ld /home/metricsagent` -- notice it displays as owned by `logshipper` (the first name that resolves for that UID), even though it's metricsagent's own home directory.

Decide which account should keep 1301 (the original, `logshipper`, which already owns real data at `/var/lib/logship/data`) and give the other one a fresh, unused UID instead of touching the account that's actually correct.

`sudo usermod -u 1302 metricsagent` (pick any UID not already in use -- check `getent passwd | awk -F: '{print $3}'` first). Verify: `id logshipper`, `id metricsagent` now show different UIDs, and `ls -ld /home/metricsagent` shows it owned by `metricsagent` again (usermod re-chowns the account's own home directory to the new UID automatically).
